query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase, compositionally complex HEA, service exposure (e.g., prolonged high-temperature or stress conditions) can trigger short-range ordering that leads to the nucleation and gradual coalescence of a brittle intermetallic phase (such as a Laves or B2 structure) within the grain interiors. If the volume fraction of this ordered phase exceeds a percolation threshold, the continuous matrix responsible for ductility is disrupted, and crack propagation is facilitated along the ordered regions, leading to measurable toughness degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially homogeneous, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a refractory HEA with a disordered BCC or FCC matrix) with chemical complexity that suppresses conventional grain‐boundary segregation.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging or service loading at temperatures (or under stress conditions) that promote ordering and precipitation kinetics within the alloy without invoking significant grain-boundary segregation.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant temperatures and/or mechanical loading regimes that are high enough to stimulate atomic mobility for ordering (but below melting) yet not so extreme as to trigger other degradation mechanisms; comparison with an alloy kept at a lower temperature/control condition to prevent ordering.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and eventual coalescence of nano- to microscale ordered domains (e.g., Laves or B2 phase) that begin to interconnect within the initially ductile matrix.
generation.mechanism: Short-range ordering induced by thermal or loading exposure leads to nucleation of a brittle intermetallic phase within the grain interiors. As this phase grows and becomes interconnected (reaching a percolation threshold), it interrupts the continuous ductile matrix and provides preferential paths for crack propagation, thereby degrading toughness in a way that contrasts with conventional alloys where grain-boundary segregation predominates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline single-phase alloy, the aged/exposed samples will show (a) detectable ordered phase precipitates in the matrix (via TEM/XRD), (b) a shift in fracture mode from ductile/mixed (with crack deflection by a continuous ductile phase) to more intergranular or cleavage-dominated brittle fracture, and (c) a reduced fracture strain (toughness) while retaining or even slightly enhancing yield strength due to precipitation hardening.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or solution-treated single-phase HEA exhibiting an optimal balance of strength and ductility with no detectable secondary phases.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions where the alloy is exposed to service temperatures (or stress conditions) that allow ordering kinetics to become operative. It does not account for degradation modes due to conventional grain-boundary segregation, which are suppressed in these HEAs.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of short-range ordering, the critical volume fraction at which a continuous brittle network forms, and the magnitude of the toughness reduction are uncertain and likely depend sensitively on the specific alloy composition and service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same single-phase HEA composition. Subject one set to prolonged annealing or mechanical loading at a temperature that is known (or predicted) to stimulate ordering (the experimental group), while keeping the other set at a lower temperature/control condition to maintain the single-phase state. After treatment, perform detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM and XRD) to detect any formation of ordered intermetallic phases and then conduct standardized mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness, compression, or tensile tests) to measure changes in ductility and failure mode.
measurements: Quantification of ordered phase volume fraction via XRD/TEM
Fracture mode analysis via microscopic examination of fracture surfaces
Mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility/fracture strain, and toughness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental group shows no significant formation of an ordered brittle phase or if the mechanical tests do not reveal a statistically significant reduction in toughness compared to the control group, then the hypothesis that short-range ordering and intermetallic coalescence lead to brittle behavior in the HEA is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s).
